oneSentence: The share of real positive cases that a system successfully flags.
plainExplanation:
Recall measures how well a system finds the cases you care about. A “positive case” means the kind of item you want the system to catch, such as harmful content, fraud, or consultations that mention access barriers.

You start with items that already have a correct label, often called the ground truth. The system checks those items and marks some as positive. Recall looks only at the items that truly are positive, then asks: how many of those did the system catch?

The calculation is true positives divided by all real positives. True positives are cases that really were positive and were correctly flagged. If there are many false negatives, meaning real positives the system missed, recall goes down.

High recall matters when missing a real case is costly. But recall alone does not tell you how many false alarms the system creates. That is why it is often discussed alongside precision, which asks a different question.

everydayAnalogy.title: Finding all the forms about blocked access
everydayAnalogy.story: A city office receives 200 public feedback forms after a transport consultation. Staff want to find every form that mentions blocked access for older persons or persons with disabilities. They use a keyword tool to pull out likely matches for review. If 40 forms truly mention blocked access and the tool finds 32 of them, its recall is based on those 32 found out of the 40 that really mattered.

mapping.analogyElement: all forms that truly mention blocked access
8 relevant forms left in the pile

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A keyword tool is much simpler than many AI systems. Real models may use patterns learned from data, may behave differently on new data, and may involve a threshold that changes recall, so the office example does not show the full mechanics.

visual.title: Precision–recall threshold simulator
visual.learningObjective: After using this explainer, the reader should be able to say that recall is the proportion of real positive cases found, and that changing the decision threshold can raise recall while also affecting precision.
visual.description: Show a horizontal threshold slider above a row or scatter of scored items. Each item has a true label known to the explainer: positive items in one shape or colour, negative items in another. As the slider moves, items on one side of the threshold become ‘flagged’. Counters update live for true positives, false positives and false negatives, and the displayed recall value changes accordingly. A companion precision value can also update so readers can compare the two measures without confusing them.

steps.label: See the scored items
steps.explanation: The explainer starts with items that each have a model score and a known true label. Some are truly positive and some are not.
steps.visualInstruction: Render 20 to 40 small SVG marks arranged by score from low to high. Use both colour and shape so true positives and true negatives remain distinguishable without relying on colour alone.

steps.label: Set the threshold
steps.explanation: The threshold decides which items the system flags as positive. Lowering it usually flags more items.
steps.visualInstruction: Provide a draggable vertical line or range input tied to the score axis. Mark all items above the threshold as flagged with an outline or check icon.

steps.label: Watch recall change
steps.explanation: Recall rises when more of the truly positive items are caught, and falls when more are missed.
steps.visualInstruction: Update a formula panel in plain text: recall = true positives / all real positives. Animate number changes if motion is allowed; otherwise swap values instantly.

steps.label: Compare with precision
steps.explanation: A lower threshold can improve recall but may also create more false alarms. This shows why recall and precision answer different questions.
steps.visualInstruction: Display precision beside recall with a short note under each metric. Optionally highlight false positives and false negatives in different patterns.

visual.interaction: Readers drag a threshold slider left or right, or use keyboard arrow keys on the focused range control, to see how the set of flagged items changes and how recall and precision update together.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This interactive shows a set of items with known true labels and model scores. You control a threshold that decides which items are flagged as positive. When you lower the threshold, more items are flagged. This usually catches more of the truly positive items, so recall often increases, but it can also flag more items that are not truly positive. The explainer reports the current counts of true positives, false positives and false negatives, and states recall as the number of true positives divided by the total number of truly positive items. Its main lesson is that recall measures missed real cases, not false alarms.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: Readers see the same scored items, threshold control and metric values, but changes happen without animation. When the threshold moves, the highlighted items and the recall and precision numbers update instantly in a static layout.

workedExample.scenario: The duty officer evaluates the classifier against 100 passages from a cleared test set. Desk officers have confirmed that 20 passages contain commitments requiring follow-up.
workedExample.input: 100 test passages, including 20 actual positive cases.
process: The classifier flags 25 passages at the selected threshold.
Reviewers confirm that 16 of the flagged passages contain follow-up commitments. These are true positives.
Because the test set contains 20 actual positives, the classifier missed 4 of them. These are false negatives.
workedExample.result: Recall is 80%. At this threshold, the classifier catches 16 of the 20 passages that require follow-up and misses 4. The 9 irrelevant passages it also flagged affect precision, not recall.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A duty officer in a regional bureau is finalising a note for the file following a bilateral. Before close of business, an approved classifier flags passages that may record commitments requiring follow-up by desk officers.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Recall shows what share of the passages confirmed by reviewers as containing follow-up commitments the classifier actually flagged. Low recall means genuine commitments are being missed, even if every passage it did flag appears relevant. The result applies at the threshold tested.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Bilateral notes may contain confidential or politically sensitive material. They must not be uploaded to a public or otherwise unapproved tool. Testing must use an environment approved for that material, or suitably cleared or synthetic text, and the classifier must not replace review by the responsible desk officer.

whyItMatters: If a system misses too many real cases, a good-looking overall score can hide a serious failure. Recall helps people judge whether the system is safe enough for tasks where missed cases have real consequences.
whereYouMayHearIt: An ICT governance board reviewing test results before approving a pilot
A vendor demonstration to a procurement unit for a document-screening tool
An evaluation office discussing a model validation report
An inter-agency working group setting the threshold for a referral tool

commonMisconceptions.misconception: High recall means the system is generally accurate.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not necessarily. A system can catch most real positive cases and still make many false alarms. Recall looks at missed real cases, not overall correctness.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Recall and precision are just two words for the same score.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They answer different questions. Recall asks how many real positive cases were found, while precision asks how many flagged cases were actually positive.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If recall is 90%, the system is right 90% of the time.
commonMisconceptions.correction: No. A recall of 90% means it found 90% of the real positive cases. It says nothing by itself about negatives or about how many flagged cases were wrong.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Recall tells you how good a system is at catching the cases you do not want to miss.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: Recall, also called sensitivity or true positive rate, is TP / (TP + FN): the proportion of actual positive instances that the classifier labels positive at a given threshold.

keyTakeaway: Recall asks: among all the cases that were truly positive, what proportion did the system flag at the chosen threshold?

quickCheck.question: A system reviews 50 documents. Ten truly contain a problem that should be flagged. It correctly flags 8 of those 10. What is its recall?
quickCheck.explanation: Recall is true positives divided by all real positives. Here that is 8 divided by 10, so the recall is 80%. The total number of documents does not matter for this calculation.

issues.problem: The items do not start as “true positives” and “true negatives”. Before the threshold is applied, they are actual positives and actual negatives. True positive and true negative describe combinations of the known label and the threshold-based prediction. This wording teaches the confusion-matrix categories incorrectly.
issues.fix: Render 20 to 40 small SVG marks arranged by score from low to high. Use both colour and shape so actual positives and actual negatives remain distinguishable without relying on colour alone.

issues.problem: The evaluation unit shifts from phrases to drafts. The scenario says the tool flags phrases, but the relevance statement describes recall as the share of drafts caught. Those are different evaluations unless a rule for classifying whole drafts is stated.
issues.fix: Recall helps the team judge whether the tool is catching most phrases that really differ from agreed language. High recall may matter if missing non-agreed wording could create diplomatic or operational problems.
